references.text: The continuation of this event, where Jesus tells Simon not to be afraid and that from now on he will catch people.

Simon Peter's reaction to the miraculous catch of fish – he falls at Jesus' knees and asks him to go away because he is a sinful man. The verse just before explains why they were filled with amazement.
A similar reaction of amazement (θάμβος) among the people after Jesus cast out an unclean spirit – they were seized with wonder at his authority and power.
The people were filled with amazement and awe (θάμβος) after the healing of the lame man at the Beautiful Gate, a similar response to God's miraculous work.
Job describes God as doing great and unfathomable things beyond number – a background for wonder at God's mighty works, just as the fishermen experienced during the miraculous catch.

When the Lord brought back those who were captive in Zion, their mouths were filled with laughter and shouts of joy; the nations said that the Lord had done great things. It expresses the overwhelming reaction when God acts powerfully.
A similar miraculous catch of fish after Jesus' resurrection, where the disciples cast the net on the right side and caught a huge number of fish – parallel to the event in Luke 5.
The net was full of 153 large fish but did not tear – parallel to the miraculous catch in Luke 5 where the nets were beginning to break.
Mark's account of the calling of Simon, Andrew, James, and John by the Sea of Galilee – parallel to the event where Jesus calls fishermen to follow him.
Matthew's account of the calling of the first disciples by the Sea of Galilee, who left their nets and followed Jesus – a parallel context to the miraculous catch of fish in Luke 5.
Habakkuk describes the enemy's fishing with nets as a metaphor; God's sovereignty over the sea and its creatures forms a thematic background for Jesus' lordship over the fish.
